250	## Two layers of code
251	
252	The repository holds two layers of code. Different tools build them, at different times, so "compile" means a different thing in each layer.
253	
254	The implementation is the parser, walk, the compiled checker, the code generator and the run time. It is the Java and Scala under `ProjectFortress/src/`, with the parser grammars (`parser/*.rats`) and the syntax tree generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`. `ant compileAll` builds it into `ProjectFortress/build/` ("Building", below). `ant compile` is another name for it.
255	
256	The Fortress code is the library, the tests and the programs: the `.fss` and `.fsi` files. The `fortress` commands run the phases on it and keep the results in the caches:
257	
258	- Walk runs the phases on each component that a run needs. It needs no `fortress compile`.
259	- `fortress compile` writes a component's jar. It is for the compiled path's components only: the compiler's library, compiled tests and compiled programs.
260	- `fortress run` compiles no Fortress source.
261	- A command reuses an entry if no source that the entry depends on is newer than the entry: its own source, and the `.fsi` files of the apis that it imports, at any depth.
262	
263	An edit makes stale what was built from it:
264	
265	- Java or Scala: the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/`. Run `ant compileAll`. The cache entries that the edited code wrote are stale too, and no entry notices it: an entry is compared with its sources, never with the implementation. For example, after a change to a native helper's signature, its old wrapper stays in `nativewrapper_cache/`, and the run links the old signature. For this reason, the build deletes the caches when the implementation changes ("Building").
266	- A parser grammar: the generated parser, and every entry that it parsed. Run `ant compileAll`.
267	- A `.fss` or `.fsi` file of the library: the entries of that component, and after an `.fsi` edit, the entries of every component that imports the api. Walk analyses them again by itself. A component of the compiler's library needs a compile, or the library order ("After an edit of the library").
268	- A test or a program: its own entries. Walk and the harness analyse a walk test again by themselves. Compile a compiled test or program again, or let the harness do it.
269	
270	## The caches
271	
272	All the caches are gitignored. A caches folder also holds:
273	
274	- `environment_cache/`: another cache of walk's.
275	- `nativewrapper_cache/`: the wrappers for the Java classes that an api imports with `import java`.
276	- `global.map`: the linker's saved state, an empty map in practice. If it is missing, the linker writes an empty one, also in a private caches folder.
277	- `implementation.stamp`: the stamp of the build that the caches belong to ("Building", below).
278	
279	Only these runs read `default_repository/caches`: `fortress compile`, `fortress run`, `fortress junit` (and `junit.sh`), `ant testOnly`, and a direct walk run. These runs use private caches (`-Dfortress.caches` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`), and need neither the library order nor warm caches: `harness-one.sh`, the gate's ladder regression (`gate.md`) and both ant suites. `harness-one.sh` keeps its private cache beside its scratch folder between calls (`tests-running.md`).
280	
281	## The library order
282	
283	The first of its compiles, `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, holds the top type `Any`, which both libraries share. The other four are the compiler's own. All five take about 100 to 110 s after `ant compileAll`.
284	
285	Run it only when the caches lack the library's jars, or hold stale ones:
286	
287	- after a build that printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, and in a tree whose caches are empty;
288	- after an edit of a library `.fsi` that the section "After an edit of the library" names.
289	
290	Otherwise the jars are in place, and a compiled test or program needs no library order. The five commands:
291	
292	    cd ProjectFortress
293	    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss            # 17 s
294	    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss    # 63 s
295	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss        # 27 s
296	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss        # 2 s
297	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss         # 2 s
298	
299	Before the first compiled run, check that `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/` holds five jars: `fortress.AnyType.jar`, `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`, `fortress.CompilerLibrary.jar`, `fortress.CompilerAlgebra.jar` and `CompilerSystem.jar`, which has no prefix. Sometimes all five compiles exit 0 and a jar is missing. The cause is not known.
300	
301	- If a jar is missing, run the five commands again. Once, this made the jars.
302	- If a jar is still missing, report it as a defect. Quote the commands, their exit codes and the folder's listing.
303	- Keep the caches in this case too. Once, emptying them made the jars, but a deletion hides the cause.
304	
305	## Name resolution
306	
307	- `fortress.source.path` searches `.` (the current directory) first, then `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin`, `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/test_library`. The first `Foo.fsi` or `Foo.fss` that it finds wins. So a file in the directory that you run from hides the library's file of the same name.
308	- A component's file name without `.fss` must be the component's name.
309	- If both libraries use one api name, one of them breaks. For this reason, the compiler's apis have the `Compiler` prefix.
310	- The top-level `CompilerLibrary/` holds `.fsi`-only stubs, not `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss`. `lib/` holds Fortress sources, not jars.
311	- If paths behave wrongly, read `repository/ProjectProperties.java`. It resolves `FORTRESS_HOME`, `BASEDIR` and the cache paths.
312	
313	## Building
314	
315	Run `ant compileAll` from the tree's root. It is the only build: `ProjectFortress/build.xml` is a stub.
316	
317	- It makes the parser and the syntax tree again only if their sources changed.
318	- javac compiles only the changed Java files and the files that depend on them. scalac runs only if its inputs changed, and then compiles every Scala file.
319	- It decides by a stamp whether it deletes the caches. `ProjectFortress/build/implementation.stamp` is a hash of the built implementation, and each caches folder holds the stamp of the build that filled it. At its end, the build keeps `default_repository/caches` if its stamp equals the new one, and empties it if not. It does not touch a private caches folder. It prints `Caches <folder> kept` or `Caches <folder> started again, empty`. The comment "The caches and the implementation" in `build.xml` gives the rule.
320	- `ant cleanCache` deletes the caches, whatever their stamp.
321	- With nothing changed, it takes about 4 s. After an edit, it takes about 25 to 60 s on an idle machine, scalac about 19 s of it, and about 50 to 80 s on a new or cleaned tree. While other agents build, it takes up to about 140 s.
322	- After a build that started the caches again, yours or a test target's, run the library order before the next compiled run. So each edit of Java or Scala costs about 2 to 3 minutes before a compiled run: the build, then the library order.
323	- If it fails, fix the error and run the same command again. Clear nothing by hand.
324	
325	## After an edit of the library
326	
327	The compiled path sees an edit of its library only when you compile the edited component itself. Compiling your own program never recompiles the library under it.
328	
329	- If you edited the `.fss` of one of the five library components, and not its `.fsi`: run `fortress compile` on that component only. Programs need no recompile.
330	- If you edited the `.fsi` of AnyType, CompilerBuiltin, CompilerLibrary or CompilerAlgebra: run the whole library order. Every api depends on these four.
331	- If you edited `CompilerSystem.fsi`: compile CompilerSystem only.
332	- If you edited any other file of `Library/` or `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: it is walk's library. Do nothing: walk reads it again, and compiled programs do not link it yet.
333	
334	## Symptoms of a skipped step
335	
336	If you skip the step for your edit, the run shows it:
337	
338	- After an edit of a body, the run uses the old code and gives no warning.
339	- After an edit of an api, the run stops with `NoSuchMethodError` or `NoClassDefFoundError` on a library member. Examples: `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.println`, `coerce_ZZ32`, `fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32`. The run found no library jar and used the bootstrap stubs: old class files of the compiler's library that the build compiles from `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/` into `ProjectFortress/build/fortress/`.
340	
341	If you see either, do the step now: recompile the component, or run the library order. Do not delete the caches to fix it. A deletion works only because it repeats the library order and every analysis from cold. If something else looks like a stale cache, find its cause before you delete anything.
342	
343	Two messages look like a skipped step, but usually show a defect:
344	
345	- A `NoSuchMethodError` on a method of your own program, often with a mangled name such as `\=tag?1??Arrow...`, is a defect of the compiled path. Record it (`tests-writing.md`).
346	- "Unable to read serialized data for X, recommend you delete the Fortress bytecode cache and relink" is usually a defect of the code generator. Search the gap ledger for the message. Run the library order only if X is a member of a `Compiler*` or `AnyType` component. Keep the caches, whatever the message advises.
347	
348	Two more facts help you read a run:
349	
350	- A `fortress compile` of a source that did not change, and whose jar exists, writes nothing and exits 0.
351	- A library compile that failed or was killed wrote nothing, or only its jar. Programs link the old jar with no warning until you fix the error and compile that component again.
352

# Running tests

**track**
: One of the four JVMs of `ant testFast`.

**shard**
: One of the four JVMs of `ant testSystem`. Shard i of n takes every n-th file of the sorted list, from index i.

**code state**
: Code of a tree as one edit leaves it. Only an edit of code makes a new code state; a commit does not.

## The two suites

`ant testFast` runs about 2,100 tests in four tracks at once, in about 5 to 7 minutes:

- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
- misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes.

`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs about 680 tests in four shards, in about 2 to 4 minutes.

`ant testSpecData` runs the specification's 130 extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk, in about a minute. The gate runs it after the two suites.

The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:

    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'

The two suites work in the same way:

- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, as every `ant` test target does, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.
- Each JVM gets 768 MB, a 32 MB stack and `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, whatever the shell exports. The run steps of the compiled tests get `JAVA_FLAGS=-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, also whatever the shell exports.
- Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts. Each JVM keeps its caches in a folder of its own under it, so that the JVMs do not overwrite each other's entries. Temporary files go to `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
- The results are in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-<track>/` and `system-<i>/`, as `TEST-<class>.txt`.

To run a suite:

- Run one suite at a time in a tree, because each suite deletes the `test-caches` that the other uses.
- Read the verdict in the line before `Total time:`: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures, and `BUILD FAILED` means at least one. Every `ant` test target ends with these lines, and exits non-zero when it failed.
- To compare test counts, compare the sum of the four shards. A file added to `tests/` moves every later file to another shard.
- If a suite's count fell, a `.test` file or a `tests=` line almost always went missing.

## The switches that the harness reads

Put a `-D` switch on the `java` line of a run by hand; the `java` line in `harness-one.sh` is a model. On the `ant` line, it does not reach the suites' JVMs.

- `-Dtests=<dir>`: the folder that `SystemJUTest` runs, in place of `tests/`.
- `-Dfortress.suite.shard=i/n`: run shard i of n only.
- `-Dfortress.unittests.count=N`: run N files at most.
- `-Dfortress.unittests.seed=<value>`: the order of the files. Each run prints its seed as `FORTRESS_UNITTESTS_SEED=...`.
- `FORTRESS_JUNIT_VERBOSE=1` for `SystemJUTest`, `-Dfortress.junit.verbose=true` for the compiled tests' classes: show the output of passing tests too.
- `-Dfortress.junit.reset=false`: `CompilerJUTest` and `LibraryJUTest` keep their caches folder. Without it, they empty it when they start.

## Outside the gate

- `ant testNotPassing` runs the interpreter programs of `ProjectFortress/not_passing_yet/`, which are expected to fail. It fails if one of them passes.
- No suite and no stage of the gate runs the team demos, the programs of `ProjectFortress/demos/`. Keep each of the 52 demos that `DemoTests` lists reaching its end (P-79). Check them with the demo driver below, not with `ant testDemos`, whose test of the output is weaker:
  - If your change edits walk, the parser, a phase that both paths run or the interpreter's library, run the driver once, after your last edit of code.
  - Print the driver with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-team-demos/REPORT.md#Commands worked out'`. Save the first script that it prints, under "The demo driver", without the text around it, as `tmp/run-demos.sh` in your tree.
  - From the tree's root, after you set up the call, run `bash tmp/run-demos.sh tmp/demos`. It runs long, so run it in the background with a log (`session.md`, "Long commands"). It runs the demos under walk one at a time and writes `tmp/demos/summary.tsv`.
  - The driver's last line of output, before the log's `EXIT=` line, must read 'demos: 52 run, 52 reached their end'. A demo reaches its end if it exits 0 and its output holds no "fail" in upper or lower case.
  - If your change breaks a demo and you know how to repair the demo, repair it in the commit of your change. Otherwise, report the demo, its output and the ledger row that holds the missing feature, as a defect that your change makes or uncovers.
- Nothing runs these folders: `not_working_compiler_tests/`, `not_working_library_tests/`, `not_working_static_tests/`, `obsolete_interpreter_tests/`, `long_term_not_working/`, `linker_tests/`, `compiler_regressions/`. Put every new test in a gated test folder. A test of a defect that fails today is an `XXX` test there (`tests-writing.md`).

## When to run a whole suite

- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.
- If your edit changes the Java or Scala of the checker, of walk or of a phase that both paths share, run all the tests that it reaches. Run them once, after your last edit of code. The run needs no commit.
  - For the checker, run `ant testQuick`: the compiler, othercompiler and library tracks at once (below).
  - For walk, run `ant testSystem`. It is the same as its four shards run by hand.
  - For a shared phase (under `compiler/`: name binding, DSL grammars, desugaring, the marking of overloaded calls in `OverloadRewriter`) or the parser, run both.
- Quote the verdict lines and the command in your report, with the commit if your code is committed.
- If the gate later runs on a tree that holds other changes too, that tree is another code state. Your run and the gate's run do not repeat each other.
- After an edit of the code generator (`codegen/`, `OverloadSet`) or the run time (`runtimeSystem/`), run your own tests, and the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`) if `compiler.md` asks for them. Leave the whole tracks to the gate.
- After every other change, run only your own tests, through the scripts below, and the demos where "Outside the gate" asks for them. Leave the rest to the gate. This includes an edit of either library, though it reaches many tests.

The suites do not check these:

- the bytecode optimizer, which nothing in the compiler calls;
- DSL grammars, except one program whose phases the misc track runs: `syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss`;
- the linker's aliasing of apis;
- `fortress unparse`;
- the round trip of the `.tfi` and `.tfs` caches;
- a behaviour above one thread that one run of each suite at four threads does not hit.

If your edit is in one of these, your own tests are its only check. Say so in your report.

## One test, or a few

Each script and `fortress junit` below ends with the verdict of JUnit's text runner: `OK (n tests)`, or `FAILURES!!!` with the counts. Read the verdict there: the exit code is 0 whatever the verdict.

### Interpreter tests

Run interpreter tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`) from the tree's root, after you set up the call:

    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh <tree>/tmp/h1 \
        ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss [ProjectFortress/tests/X.test] [more files ...]

- It runs `SystemJUTest` with testSystem's JVM settings, at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, on a folder that holds only the files that you name.
- It keeps its cache in the folder `<scratch-dir>.cache`. It starts from that cache while the build and the library sources are those that filled it. Otherwise, or with `COLD_CACHE=1`, it starts empty. Its first line says `cache filled` or `cache empty`.
- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing. After you edit Java, Scala or a parser grammar, run `ant compileAll` first. If your tree has no build, seed it or build it as `worktrees.md` says.
- Give it a scratch directory that holds nothing else. The script deletes the directory when it starts and when it ends.
- If a test has an `X.test` file (its keys for a refusal at load), name it beside its `X.fss`.
- It takes 15 to 25 s with an empty cache, mostly to analyse the library, and about 4 s with a filled one. Name several files in one call to run them in one JVM.
- It shows the output of passing tests too, and removes the Java stack frames.

To see the whole diagnostic, with its Java stack, run the program directly, from `ProjectFortress/` as the harness does, because an import is looked up in the current directory first:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress -debug stacktrace tests/X.fss

The direct run and the harness use different heaps (`interpreter.md`, "Running a program").

### Compiled tests

Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`).

The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.

    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
        ProjectFortress/compiler_tests X.test Y.test > <tree>/tmp/junit-<label>.txt 2>&1

- `<label>` is any word. It marks the run's lines in the output. The script writes to standard output only, so redirect it to your `tmp/`.
- With `ONE_JVM=1`, the whole list runs in one `fortress junit` run, in one JVM. The compile and link tests run before the run tests, as in the suite. Without `ONE_JVM=1`, each file gets its own JVM.
- It removes the named components' entries from the tree's `default_repository/caches` before the whole list and after it, not between files. So a link test and the run test that uses its jar pass in one call, with or without `ONE_JVM=1`.
- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing, as `harness-one.sh` does.
- It removes the Java stack frames, and cuts each line at 240 characters.
- Its JVMs keep their temporary files in the tree's `tmp/`, and run at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`.

To run the same list in one JVM without the script, and without its removal of cache entries:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress junit compiler_tests/X.test compiler_tests/Y.test

Run all the new files of one test folder together, in one JVM, as the suite does. A test that passes alone can fail beside others.

## One unit-test class, or one track

To run one unit-test class: `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=BitsJUTest`. It uses the tree's own caches and the shell's `FORTRESS_THREADS`.

To run tracks of testFast whole, run their target. Each target runs its tracks as testFast does, with the same JVMs and private caches:

- `ant testCompiler`: the compiler and othercompiler tracks.
- `ant testOtherCompiler`: the othercompiler track.
- `ant testLibrary`: the library track.
- `ant testQuick`: the three tracks.
# The interpreter (walk)

Walk's code is in `interpreter/`:

- `evaluator/`: the tree walker.
- `env/`: the environments, which map names to values, and the wrappers that load components and apis.
- `rewrite/`: walk's own rewrite of the tree.
- `glue/`: the natives.

## How walk evaluates a program

After the phases (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"), walk rewrites each component in `interpreter/rewrite/`: it gives each reference to a name the lexical depth of its declaration. The evaluator looks up the name by that depth. The compiled path has no such rewrite.

At a call of a generic function, walk infers the static arguments from the run-time types of the arguments (`interpreter/evaluator/EvaluatorBase.java`, `inferAndInstantiateGenericFunction`). Each static parameter gets an interval, from a lower to an upper bound, in a `LatticeIntervalMap` (`useful/`). A type in the domain of an arrow type, such as `T` in `T -> ZZ32`, is contravariant. So its bounds go into the dual map, `LatticeIntervalMapDual`: the same table, with the order reversed. `MakeInferenceSpecific` then makes the inferences more specific, in practice only in the dual map.

Walk chooses a coercion by the value at run time. The specification and the compiled path choose it statically. Walk has no static types, so it cannot choose statically. The expected-failure tests `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticRungC.fss` and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC.fss` record the difference.

## Where a fix of walk belongs

Both paths run the same desugaring phases. Inside them, switches in `Shell.java` decide which desugarings run. Walk turns off these desugarings, which the compiled path runs:

- coercion;
- chained comparisons;
- compound and tuple assignment, and subscripts;
- case expressions, typecase and type ascription;
- the marking of a bodiless declaration as abstract.

Walk evaluates those nodes itself, in `interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java` (`forChainExpr`, `forAssignment`, `forCaseExpr`, `forTypecase`, `forAsExpr`). It converts by coercion at dispatch, in `OverloadedFunction.bestMatchWithCoercion`. So if walk is wrong on one of these nodes, fix the evaluator, not the desugarer.

An edit of a phase that both paths run, or of the desugaring switches, can change both paths. An edit under `interpreter/` changes walk only.

## What walk checks

Walk does not check static types (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"). The commands that stop after a phase, and `unparse`, use the compiler's prelude and the compiled path's desugaring switches (`compiler.md`, "The `fortress` commands"). So `fortress typecheck` does not check a walk program, and `desugar` or `unparse` does not print the tree that walk runs. That tree is the component's entry in `interpreter_cache/` (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").

Under walk, the disambiguator, the phase that binds names, refuses a program's own top-level type that has the name of a type of `FortressLibrary`, such as `Index` or `Indexed`: "Type name may refer to: Index, FortressLibrary.Index". Give such a type another name.

At load, walk checks the overload sets, some `comprises` clauses, inherited abstract methods and `override` declarations. It lifts each object expression to the top level as an object, which takes the static parameters of an enclosing generic function, and checks it as an object. It checks a trait or object with static parameters once, through a stand-in: one type for all its instances, with a symbolic type for each static parameter (`symbolicInstance` in `interpreter/evaluator/BuildEnvironments.java`). Through the stand-in, it does not check two functional methods whose parameter types mention a symbolic type. It makes no stand-in, and so checks nothing through one, for a declaration with an `opr` static parameter, or where its static parameters, `where` clause or `extends` clause raise an error at the symbolic types. It refuses:

- two declarations of one name that its parameter-by-parameter check cannot order. It accepts them if `comprises` clauses cover the overlap. For every pair of functions of which at least one is generic, it checks the overloading rules of `SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language", on their declared domains (`revival-changes.md`, "Dispatch and overloading"): the No Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the Return Type Rule. So it refuses two whose declared domains are equal. The message names the rule: "fails because their parameter lists have the same types", "fails the Return Type Rule" or "fails the Meet Rule". Walk keeps the team's check and messages for the pairs below. The team's check looks for a position where the two parameter types neither nest nor exclude. If a parameter type there mentions a static parameter, the message is "at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types". If neither does, it is "are unrelated (neither subtype, excludes, nor equal) and no excluding pair is present". The pairs:
  - a pair with a varargs parameter;
  - a pair whose parameter lists differ in length, only where one of them has a varargs parameter. Walk checks no other pair of lists of different lengths;
  - a pair that is neither two generic declarations nor a generic one beside a plain one;
  - the instances of an explicit instantiation.

  Where it reads exclusion over the whole tuple of parameter types, at the instance that the equalities force, it reads two parameter types that still mention a static parameter as excluding only where no instances of the two can meet. Walk departs from the rules in these cases:
  - At load, it does not check two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains. It compares them at each call, on the instance that the call makes. So such a pair that breaks the rules loads, and a call can fail with "Cannot find definition for method" (ledger row 780).
  - It refuses two generic functional methods whose declared domains lie one inside the other, in a type without static parameters (ledger row 779).
  - It refuses a pair whose overlap it finds only through an instance of a supertype, also where a third declaration covers the overlap (ledger row 539).
  - It refuses overloads on two instantiations of one generic type, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])` (ledger row 416).
  - Its parameter-by-parameter check reads an object type over a static parameter as excluding a type that one of its instances is or extends. So it loads `g[\T\](x: Box[\T\], y: ZZ32)` beside `g(x: Box[\ZZ32\], y: Any)`, which the Meet Rule refuses (ledger row 788).
  - It reads no `where` clause when it reads exclusion over the whole tuple. So it refuses such a pair where one declaration has a `where` clause of its own (ledger row 787).
  - Where a program's own component declares both, it refuses a generic operator between an array of a number type and a number, on either side, beside the operator of a self-typed trait, as `AdditiveGroup`'s `+`: "at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types". The checker accepts such a pair, and the library's own pairs load (ledger row 804).
  - It loads a function over `Index` beside one over a pair whose element types neither lie below `Index` nor exclude it, which the Meet Rule refuses (ledger row 806).
  - It loads a type that provides two functional symbolic operators, such as two `||`, that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`). The checker refuses the pair (ledger row 611).

  The paths differ on `f[\T extends { K, R[\T\] }\](x: T)` beside `f(x: Z)`, where `K comprises { A, B, C }`, `Z excludes { A, B }`, and `C` is an object that extends `Z` but not `R`. Walk refuses the pair: "fails the Meet Rule". The checker reads the bounds, finds that no value lies in both domains, and accepts it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 713).
- two functional methods that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods in a type that provides both, where their name is an identifier or an operator named by a word, as `MAX`.
- an overloaded function with one parameter of type `T`, where `T extends Any` is written: `f[\T extends Any\](x: T)`.
- an extender that a `comprises` clause of the program's main component does not allow. Walk does not yet check the library's clauses, another component's clauses or an object expression's clauses. Where a listed type names a bounded type `where`-clause variable, as `NBox[\E\]` in `comprises { NBox[\E\] } where [\E extends Number\]`, walk ignores the variable's bound, and runs `NBox[\String\]` (ledger row 754). In another declaration's bound, it takes a name equal to the variable's as the variable (ledger row 778).
- a trait whose `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, where a member's declared type names the variable: "Missing type E" (ledger row 755).
- an object or object expression without static parameters that inherits an abstract method and does not define it. Bodies define it if they are at or below its parameter types and together cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. Walk also refuses where its search for a cover does not settle: at a cycle of `comprises` clauses, at a symbolic type, or beyond 10,000 steps or 4,096 combinations of listed types. It also refuses a valid object whose one body for the method has a static parameter of its own (ledger row 728).
- a declaration with the modifier `override`, in a trait, object or object expression, that overrides no declaration that its type's immediate supertraits provide. An `override` at an inherited declaration's own parameter types overrides nothing. At an instance of a generic trait above a declared object, equal parameter types count as overridden. Walk does not read all the bounds of the static parameters in two cases:
  - an object expression, which takes its static parameters from the function around it;
  - a generic trait or object that extends a type under a `where` clause.

  In these cases, walk does not refuse an `override` if the inherited declaration's parameter types mention a static parameter and differ from the `override`'s.

So a library edit can stop every program at load, if it does one of these:

- adds an overload;
- leaves an inherited abstract method that no bodies cover, covers it only by a body with a static parameter of its own, or covers it by bodies whose cover walk's search cannot settle;
- adds an `override` that overrides nothing;
- gives a member a type that names its trait's `comprises`-clause variable, as `E` in `AnyList`.

Walk checks a program's declarations against the library's only when it analyses the library, not when it loads the library's entries from the cache (ledger row 342). So a program that walk refuses with an empty cache runs with a filled one. Deleting the program's own entries does not bring the check back. To see such a refusal, run with an empty cache, as `COLD_CACHE=1` gives `harness-one.sh`.

`tests-writing.md` says how a test names a refusal at load.

Walk's overload-ambiguity message names its two declarations in an order that varies from run to run. On one core, the order is fixed for a given library, but a library edit can change it. Do not pin or compare this order. The harness reads only that an `XXX` test fails.

## Natives

The library binds each of walk's natives by a string in its `.fss` files: `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.X")`. The classes are in `interpreter/glue/prim/`. They take the evaluator's boxed values, so the compiled path cannot use them. `import java`, the compiled path's way to bind natives, is wired under walk but unfinished, and no test uses it.

To raise a Fortress exception that a Fortress `catch` sees, a native throws a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object. `Int.overflow()` in `Int.java` there makes one, and its callers throw it:

    FObject f = (FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(WellKnownNames.integerOverflowException);
    return new FortressError(f);

A `catch` sees no other Java exception, so any other exception from a native ends the run, a division by zero too.

## Running a program

    bin/fortress P.fss

- If the run stops on an error, it prints the error and the Fortress stack under `Context:`. The hint below them names `-debug interpreter`, which shows nothing more. To see the Java stack too, run `bin/fortress -debug stacktrace P.fss`.
- Walk searches for imports in the current directory first (`build-and-caches.md`, "Name resolution").
- If `JAVA_FLAGS` is not set, `bin/fortress` uses `-Xmx256m -Xss32m`. Your setup gives a 4 GB heap, and the test harness uses 768 MB. A test can pass at two of these heaps and die at the third. If you claim that a run fails near a memory limit, measure the claim at 256 MB: run with `JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx256m -Xss32m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"`.
- Your setup sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, the size of the pool, to 1 (`SKILL.md`, "Parallelism and mutable state"). If it is unset, the pool has half the CPUs.
- A small program takes about 8 s with cold caches, and about 4 s with warm caches.
- Do not take or record a timing of walk. Do not edit anything to make walk faster.
- To check a build, run `bin/fortress explorations/claude_demo.fss`. It prints `SUM[i <- 1#100] i = 5050` among its lines, and exits 0. `ProjectFortress/hello.fss` runs only on the compiled path.

## The model program

MicroGPT runs only under walk, by hand, never in the gate. Check the model when your brief asks for it: run your tree's `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh <work-dir> <label> [threads]`. `<work-dir>` is a folder under your tree's `tmp/`, and `threads` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, 1 by default. The script runs the quick pair at once, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`: two forward and backward passes each, against the reference values, in about 56 s for both. Each starts from an empty private cache and writes `<work-dir>/<name>.txt`. Read its `VERDICT:` line and its last line, `rc=`.

- Add the word `full` only if your brief asks for it. It runs the full pair, `MicroGptFlatCheck.fss` and `MicroGptAplCheck.fss`, with 40 checks each and a 90-minute timeout.
- If you change a line of the model, put the change in your report as a diff.

# Climb batch 22, rung R: the body errors' library text (rows 731 and 632)

- problem: the four body sites of the distance at climb batch 21b's gate, `explorations/compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv:3-6` (two `BIG MIN` at `FortressLibrary.fss:4395` and `:4401`, the fused arm at `:1466`, `List.fss:146`)

## 1. What changed and why

Three library sites that the compiled checker refuses, each a site of the distance (F-53), now write the static argument of their clause form, and `__bigOperator2`'s fused arm passes its result through `cast[\O0\]`. The text is the planner's `explorations/compile-ladder/plan-22/probes/rung-R.patch`, applied by `python3 -I explorations/compile-ladder/plan-22/probes/last5-edits.py /home/user/fortress-bodyargs min731 list731 cast46` ('applied min731 list731 cast46'). The diff's index line is the patch's, `d5abf7e6a..1997672c7`, so the patch is taken as it is.

- `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4395` and `:4401`, `String`'s `upto` and `beyond`: `n = BIG MIN[\ZZ32\][i <- self.indices, self[i]=c] i`. `BIG MIN`'s bound names its parameter (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2014`), so the checker finds no instance for an unwritten one (F-59, row 731).
- `Library/List.fss:151`, `List`'s range subscript at a stride other than 1: `<|[\E\] self[i] | i <- r |>`. The comprehension's `BIG <|[\T\]|>` is unbounded (`Library/List.fss:178`). The checker takes its bound `Any`, and the expected `List[\E\]` reaches it only where the call fails (F-221), so the body was `OR(List[\Any\], List[\E\])`.
- `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:1476`, `__bigOperator2`'s fused arm: `cast[\O0\]((outer'.unwrap)(...))`. Under the pattern `outer':BigOperator[\I0,I0,I0,L0\]` the arm's value is an `I0` where `O0` is declared (row 632, F-85). The cast is the library's device for an arm whose type the `typecase` cannot show (F-264). The team's pattern stays, and so does when the arm fuses.

Two test files are new: the walk guard `ProjectFortress/tests/WrittenReductionArgumentsWalk.fss`, and the expected failure `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXPureListStridedSubscriptWalk.fss` for the same defect left in `PureList` (section 7). One message of `ProjectFortress/tests/InferUnfixedFBoundedWalk.fss:29` is respelled, its value kept (section 6).

Commits on `wip/rung-body-arguments`: `55a87a61c` (the library and the guard) and `3f3bff4ab` (the `XXX` test).

## 2. The failing run and the passing run

The distance stage is the test of the library's sites. Its before is climb batch 21b's landed table, not run again (`explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-21b/gate/distance.txt`):

The sites are library text that only the checker reads differently: the desugared big operators are calls of the library's reduction objects, which the checker types (`explorations/coordinator/map/modules-and-phases.md:341`). The precedents, each counted in its file:

The revision box of `\secref{reduction-expr}` (`Specification/basic/expressions/reductions.tex:26-62`) says that neither implementation directs a reduction's desugaring by the type `N` of its expression yet, and: "Until the compiled type checker directs the desugaring by type, a reduction with a generator clause list whose element type no argument fixes writes its static argument in a program that both implementations are to run, as the team's own tests do" (`:51-55`). The library is such a program after the switch-over, so the edit follows the box.

The normative text gives a list expression the type `List[\T\]`, `T` the union of the types of its elements (`Specification/basic/expressions/aggregate.tex:103-105`, "List Expressions"). For `self[i]` with `self: List[\E\]` that type is `List[\E\]`, which the written `[\E\]` states.

Row 632 cites `Specification/basic/expressions/typecase.tex`, "Typecase Expressions": an arm's type is the type of its expression under the clause's binding, which shows `I0`, not `O0`.

`Specification/advanced/parallelism-locality/defining-generators.tex` and Appendix I's `\seclabel{revival-reductions}` (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:1165-1250`) were grepped for a sentence that says the library's own reductions leave the argument out (`grep -n -i 'library.*static argument\|row~731\|row~632\|upto\|__bigOperator2\|fused'`). ## 5. Walk, old against new

- The guard (section 2): its 8 string assertions pass on both trees; its stride-2 list assertions fail on the base and pass after.
- Probes (scratch, not committed), run on the base's code with `explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh /home/user/fortress-base22 <tree>/tmp/.../old-caches ListSubProbe2.fss` and on the final tree with `bin/fortress ListSubProbe2.fss`. The base:

BirdCount1q.fss`) and on the new (`../../bin/fortress BirdCount1q.fss`). Both runs exit 0 with 676 lines each, 0 differing lines (`diff`), and no "fail". The compiled checker fixes it from neither the generators, the body nor a declared type that receives the value, and refuses every such `SUM` or `PROD` that leaves it out (row 731, a gap of the checker). +component WrittenReductionArgumentsWalk
+import List.{...}
+export Executable
+
+(* String's upto and beyond answer the text before and after a character's first occurrence, and List's range subscript answers its elements at strides 1 and 2 as a list of its own element type. *)
+
+lengthOfZZ32s(xs: List[\ZZ32\]): ZZ32 = |xs|
+
+run(): () = do
+    assert("abc".upto('b'), "a", "upto of a character that occurs once answers the text before it")
+    assert("abc".beyond('b'), "c", "beyond of a character that occurs once answers the text after it")
+    assert("hello".upto('l'), "he", "upto of a character that occurs twice answers the text before its first occurrence")
+    assert("hello".beyond('l'), "lo", "beyond of a character that occurs twice answers the text after its first occurrence")
+    assert("abc".upto('z'), "abc", "upto of a character that does not occur answers the whole string")
+    assert("abc".beyond('z'), "", "beyond of a character that does not occur answers the empty string")
+    assert("abc".upto('a'), "", "upto of the first character answers the empty string")
+    assert("abc".beyond('c'), "", "beyond of the last character answers the empty string")
+
+    l = <|[\ZZ32\] 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15 |>
+    assert(l[1#3], <|[\ZZ32\] 11, 12, 13 |>, "the list at 1#3, stride 1, is its elements at 1, 2 and 3 (ranges.tex, section \"Ranges\")")

+    evens: List[\ZZ32\] = l[0:4:2]

+    assert(lengthOfZZ32s(l[1:5:2]), 3, "the list at 1:5:2 passes to a parameter declared List[\\ZZ32\\]")

+    assert(s[0#2], <|[\String\] "p", "q" |>, "the list of strings at 0#2, stride 1, is p and q (ranges.tex, section \"Ranges\")")
+    assert(s[1:3:2], <|[\String\] "q", "s" |>, "the list of strings at 1:3:2, stride 2, is q and s, a List[\\String\\] (ranges.tex, section \"Ranges\"; aggregate.tex, section \"List Expressions\")")

#!/bin/bash
# The distance stage's comparison: this table (run.sh's) against the last landed one.
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/compare.sh <last-landed-table|""> <this-table>
#
# Prints one verdict line, then every #kind and #class row whose count moved, with the
# change, and every #crash row that went or came. It is REPORTED and never red: it always
# exits 0, whatever moved, a stale shadow and a run that produced no table included (Pavol,
# answer 11, POSITIONS.md 2026-09-26: a report-only stage, whose job is driving the distance
# down). The verdicts:
#   DISTANCE DOWN|UP|SAME   <last> -> <now>
#   DISTANCE FIRST          no landed table to compare with
#   DISTANCE NO TABLE       this run produced no count, with the table's own reason
#   SETTING CHANGED         the two tables ran different settings: the counts are not like for like
#   SHADOW STALE            a shadow edit no longer matches the tracked sources
# A move of 2 to 4 errors in the components' type errors or in which pair of LEXICO, SQCAP or
# INVERSE declarations an overloading error names is the checker's run-to-run variation
# (switch-over-distance-flat.md section 5), not a change; a crash row whose line numbers
# moved because a rung edited above it prints as one gone and one new.
set -u
OLD=${1:-}; NEW=${2:?usage: compare.sh <last-landed-table> <this-table>}
field () { awk -F'\t' -v t="$1" '$1 == t { sub("^[^\t]*\t", ""); print; exit }' "$2" ; }

now=$(field '#total' "$NEW")
sh=$(field '#shadow' "$NEW")
case "$sh" in STALE*) echo "SHADOW STALE   ${sh#STALE: }" ;; esac
case "$now" in
  ''|none*) echo "DISTANCE NO TABLE   ${now:-no #total row}" ; exit 0 ;;
esac
if [ -z "$OLD" ] || [ ! -f "$OLD" ] ; then
    echo "DISTANCE FIRST   $now distinct errors, $(field '#distance' "$NEW" | cut -d';' -f1); no landed table to compare with"
    exit 0
fi
was=$(field '#total' "$OLD")
ws=$(field '#distance' "$OLD" | cut -d';' -f1); ns=$(field '#distance' "$NEW" | cut -d';' -f1)
[ "$ws" = "$ns" ] || echo "SETTING CHANGED   was $ws, now $ns: the counts below are not like for like"
case "$was" in ''|none*) echo "DISTANCE $now, the landed table has no count (${was:-no #total row})" ; exit 0 ;; esac
if   [ "$now" -lt "$was" ] ; then echo "DISTANCE DOWN   $was -> $now ($((now - was)))"
elif [ "$now" -gt "$was" ] ; then echo "DISTANCE UP   $was -> $now (+$((now - was)))"
else echo "DISTANCE SAME   $now" ; fi
awk -F'\t' '
  function key(r) { return $1 == "#kind" || $1 == "#class" || $1 == "#unit" }
  FNR == NR { if (key()) { k = substr($1, 2) " " $2 ; a[k] = $3 ; nm[k] = $4 ; ord[++n] = k }
              else if ($1 == "#crash") ca[$0] = 1 ; next }
  key() { k = substr($1, 2) " " $2 ; b[k] = $3 ; nm[k] = $4 ; if (!(k in a)) ord[++n] = k }
  $1 == "#crash" { cb[$0] = 1 }
  END {
    for (i = 1; i <= n; i++) { k = ord[i] ; if (seen[k]++) continue
      d = (b[k] + 0) - (a[k] + 0)
      if (d != 0) printf "    %-24s %6d -> %-6d (%+d)%s\n", k, a[k] + 0, b[k] + 0, d, (nm[k] != "" ? "  " nm[k] : "") }
    for (c in ca) if (!(c in cb)) { sub("^#crash\t", "", c) ; print "    crash gone   " c }
    for (c in cb) if (!(c in ca)) { sub("^#crash\t", "", c) ; print "    crash new    " c }
  }' "$OLD" "$NEW"
exit 0

(** Application of two nested BIG operators, possibly with fusion.  This only covers
    a comprehension of the form:
       BIG outer [ xs <- expr_o ] (BIG inner [x <- xs] expr_i)
    The desugarer extracts comprehensions of this form from more complex nests of
    comprehensions, using a combination of splitting:
        BIG OP [ gs_1, gs_2 ] expr = BIG OP [ gs_1 ] (BIG OP [ gs_2 ] expr)
    and filter squeezing:
        BIG OP [ xs <- g, p(xs) ] expr = BIG OP [ xs <- g.filter(p) ] expr
    There are some big caveats to this explanation in practice.  Most important is that
    we don't unlift and lift or do input/output conversion except where neccessary, so
    splitting skips these operations in between the inner and outer comprehension.
    **)
(*
This is too strong when I0 is BOTTOM.
__bigOperator2[\I0,O0,R0,L0,I1,O1 extends I0,R1,L1,E,F extends Generator[\E\]\]
              (outer:BigOperator[\I0,O0,R0,L0\],
               inner:BigOperator[\I1,O1,R1,L1\],
               gg: Generator[\F\],
               innerBody: E->I1):O0 = do
*)

              (outer:BigOperator[\I0,O0,R0,L0\],
               inner:BigOperator[\I1,O1,R1,L1\],
               gg: Generator[\F\],
               innerBody: E->I1):O0 = do
    o = outer.reduction
    i = inner.reduction
    resolvedouterBody=__resolveBottomArgumentType[\O1, I0, R0\](outer.body)
    typecase (gg,outer,inner) of
        (gg':Generator2[\E\],outer':BigOperator[\I0,I0,I0,L0\],inner':BigOperator[\I1,I0,I0,L1\]) =>
        (* Assumes that outer.body COMPOSE inner.unwrap is id
         * Often the assumption is satisfied,
         * but some types are necesary to guarantee it.
         *)
        cast[\O0\]((outer'.unwrap)(gg'.generate2[\I0,L0,L1\](outer'.reduction, inner'.reduction, fn x => (inner'.body)(innerBody(x)))))
        else =>
          ((outer.unwrap)(o.unlift(
            gg.generate[\L0\](o,fn (xs) =>
            o.lift((resolvedouterBody)(((inner.unwrap)(i.unlift(
            xs.generate[\L1\](i,fn x=> i.lift((inner.body)(innerBody(x)))))))))))))
    end
  end

typecase f of f':O1 -> R0 => fn (x:O1) : R0  => f'(x)

component NestedReductionFusion
import List.{...}
import Generator2.{...}
export Executable

(* A reduction of reductions over the prefixes of a list answers the same with and without fusion, whether or not the inner reduction distributes over the outer one. *)

sumSum(gg: Generator[\Generator[\ZZ32\]\]): ZZ32 =
    __bigOperator2[\ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,Generator[\ZZ32\]\](
        SUM[\ZZ32\](), SUM[\ZZ32\](), gg, fn (x: ZZ32): ZZ32 => x)

maxMax(gg: Generator[\Generator[\ZZ32\]\]): ZZ32 =
    __bigOperator2[\ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,Maybe[\ZZ32\],ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,Maybe[\ZZ32\],ZZ32,Generator[\ZZ32\]\](
        BIG MAX[\ZZ32\](), BIG MAX[\ZZ32\](), gg, fn (x: ZZ32): ZZ32 => x)

maxSum(gg: Generator[\Generator[\ZZ32\]\]): ZZ32 =
    __bigOperator2[\ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,Maybe[\ZZ32\],ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,Generator[\ZZ32\]\](
        BIG MAX[\ZZ32\](), SUM[\ZZ32\](), gg, fn (x: ZZ32): ZZ32 => x)

minSum(gg: Generator[\Generator[\ZZ32\]\]): ZZ32 =
    __bigOperator2[\ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,Maybe[\ZZ32\],ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,Generator[\ZZ32\]\](
        BIG MIN[\ZZ32\](), SUM[\ZZ32\](), gg, fn (x: ZZ32): ZZ32 => x)

sumProd(gg: Generator[\Generator[\ZZ32\]\]): ZZ32 =
    __bigOperator2[\ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32,Generator[\ZZ32\]\](
        SUM[\ZZ32\](), PROD[\ZZ32\](), gg, fn (x: ZZ32): ZZ32 => x)

unfused(f: Generator[\Generator[\ZZ32\]\] -> ZZ32, gg: Generator[\Generator[\ZZ32\]\]): ZZ32 = do
    switchDispatching(false)
    r = f(gg)
    switchDispatching(true)
    r
end

run(): () = do
    l = <|[\ZZ32\] 1, 3, 2 |>
    assert(unfused(sumSum, inits l), 11, "the sum of the prefix sums of 1, 3, 2 without fusion is 11")
    assert(sumSum(inits l), 11, "the sum of the prefix sums of 1, 3, 2 is 11; a sum does not distribute over a sum")
    assert(unfused(maxMax, inits l), 3, "the maximum of the prefix maxima of 1, 3, 2 without fusion is 3")
    assert(maxMax(inits l), 3, "the maximum of the prefix maxima of 1, 3, 2 is 3; a maximum does not distribute over a maximum")
    assert(unfused(maxSum, inits l), 6, "the maximum prefix sum of 1, 3, 2 without fusion is 6")
    assert(maxSum(inits l), 6, "the maximum prefix sum of 1, 3, 2 is 6")
    assert(unfused(minSum, inits l), 1, "the minimum prefix sum of 1, 3, 2 without fusion is 1")
    assert(minSum(inits l), 1, "the minimum prefix sum of 1, 3, 2 is 1")
    assert(unfused(sumProd, inits l), 10, "the sum of the prefix products of 1, 3, 2 without fusion is 10")
    assert(sumProd(inits l), 10, "the sum of the prefix products of 1, 3, 2 is 10")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

\section{Ranges}
\seclabel{ranges}

\note{Static expressions, static range types, and some range operations are not yet supported.}

\begin{Grammar}
\emph{Range} &::=& \option{\emph{Expr}}\EXP{:}\option{\emph{Expr}}\options{\EXP{:}\option{\emph{Expr}}}\\
&$|$& \emph{Expr}\EXP{\#}\emph{Expr}
\end{Grammar}

%% :
%% ::
%% ::c
%% :e
%% :e:
%% :e:e
%%
%% e:
%% e::
%% e::e
%% e:e
%% e:e:
%% e:e:e


A \emph{range expression} is used to create a special kind of \TYP{Generator} for
a set of integers, called a \TYP{Range}, useful
for indexing an array or controlling a \KWD{for} loop.  Generators in
general are discussed further in \secref{generators}.

An \emph{explicit range}
is self-contained and completely describes a set of integers.  Its
components are values of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}: assume that
$a$, $b$, and $c$ are expressions that produce such values.
An integer numeral converts to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} (\secref{literals}), and a
\KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter (\secref{natparams}) used as a component
converts to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} as an integer numeral does; it is a static error
if any other component of an explicit range has an integer type other than
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}.
\revision{revival-inference}{The revival's first revision of this section
(\secref{revival-ranges}) left open whether a \KWD{nat} parameter, which may
appear wherever a variable of type \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} can (\secref{natparams}),
may be a component of a range.
The sentence above settles it, as both implementations of the revival already
run it: the compiled type checker gives a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter used
as a value the type of a numeral, and the interpreter makes it a
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}.}

\begin{itemize}
\item The range \EXP{a\COLONOP{}b} is the set of $n=\max(0,b-a+1)$ integers $\{a, a+1, a+2, \ldots, b-2, b-1, b\}$.
This is a \emph{nonstrided} range.
If \VAR{a} and \VAR{b} are both static expressions
(described in \secref{static-expr}),
then it is a \emph{static range} of type \EXP{\TYP{StaticRange}\llbracket{}a,n,1\rrbracket}
and therefore also a \emph{range of static size} of type \EXP{\TYP{RangeOfStaticSize}\llbracket{}n\rrbracket}.

\item The range \EXP{a\COLONOP{}b\COLONOP{}c} is
the set of $n=\max\left(0, \left\lfloor {b-a+c \over c} \right\rfloor \right)$ integers
$\{a, a+c, a+2c, \ldots, a + \left\lfloor {b-a \over c} \right\rfloor c\}$,
unless $c$ is zero, in which case it throws an exception.
(If $c$ is a static expression, then it is a static error if $c$ is zero.)
This is a \emph{strided} range.
If \VAR{a}, \VAR{b}, and \VAR{c} are all static expressions,
then it is a \emph{static range} of type \EXP{\TYP{StaticRange}\llbracket{}a,n,c\rrbracket}
and therefore also a \emph{range of static size} of type \EXP{\TYP{RangeOfStaticSize}\llbracket{}n\rrbracket}.

\item The range \EXP{a\mathinner{\hbox{\tt\char'43}}n} is the set of
\EXP{\max(0,n)} integers $\{a, a+1, a+2, \ldots, a+n-3, a+n-2, a+n-1\}$.
This is a \emph{nonstrided} range.
=====
\subsection{List Expressions}
\seclabel{list-expr}

List element expressions are enclosed in
angle brackets $\llbracket$ and $\rrbracket$ and are separated by commas.
The type of a list expression is \EXP{\TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}
 where \VAR{T}
is the union type of the types of all element expressions.

A list \VAR{l} is indexed by placing an index enclosed in square brackets
immediately after an expression evaluating to \VAR{l}.
\marginnote{The new fortify fixes this.}
Thus, the index is rendered as a subscript.
Lists are always indexed from \EXP{0}.
For example:
\input{\home/basic/examples/Expr.List.tex}
evaluates to \EXP{1}.

1:<!-- The curator's decisions about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as they stand now. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- P-48 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `POSITIONS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. How the curator and the coordinator work is that skill's, and what is established is in `FACTS.md`; neither is repeated here. -->
45:- P-48 **A type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix takes its bound, never `Bottom`.** The arguments leave a parameter unfixed when it occurs only in the result type; when two arguments meet at it with no narrowest type into which both convert (a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` have one, `ZZ64`, by P-74); or when dispatch, at run time, picks a generic declaration and must choose the instance to run. Its instance is then the intersection of its upper bounds (`Any` if it has none). At checking, that is narrowed by what the call's expected type (P-49 defines it) requires of the declared return type; at run time, by the static type that the checker gave the call. It is never `Bottom`, never the union of the arguments' types, and never the value's type alone. The rule sets the instance, not which declaration runs (P-46). Why: the rule is the team's later word, from the POPL 2019 paper on multiple dispatch, and the curator trusts the team's later work above his own understanding (P-26). The rule changes nothing in microGPT, whose types are concrete. The library keeps the team's declarations of `fail`, `builtinPrimitive` and `List`'s empty comprehension, whose type parameters have no written bound, without the `extends Object` that a batch had added. Under walk, which has no static types, dispatch takes the value's type. Row 538: a compiled dispatcher that carries the static type that the checker gave the call, so that a generic declaration reached only at run time gets this instance. Rows 587, 591 and 612: three cases in which walk still gives `Bottom`.
47:- P-50 **The body of a `label` expression, and each value that an `exit` gives it, take the expected type of the whole `label`.** A `label` is a named block that code inside it can leave early with `exit`, giving a value with `with`. The specification types a `label` as the union of its body's last expression and the values that its `exit` expressions give. So when a `label` has an expected type, the compiled checker passes it into the body and into each of those values, as it does into each clause of a `typecase`. The specification's inference chapter lists the body and those values as contexts that carry an expected type. P-51 decides the same question for a call written as another call's argument. F-87 lists the checker's contexts that carry an expected type.
48:- P-51 **The checker retries a call written as another call's argument against each declaration's parameter type.** Take an outer call `f(g(x))`, whose argument is an inner call `g(x)`. If none of the compiled checker's attempts at the call accepts `f(g(x))` (P-49 gives the order of those attempts), the checker checks `g(x)` again, once for each declaration of `f`, with that declaration's parameter type at `g(x)`'s position as its expected type. The retry covers every inner call with inferred static arguments, not only one whose type parameter occurs in its result type alone. Why: the curator wants the type inference rules unified across contexts, which covers cases that the team did not build. As built, a generic declaration of `f` is first instantiated from the other arguments. A method's return type, a top-level variable, a field, an assignment, a function expression, a branch, a call's argument and another clause form's body do not direct it. == explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:7-27

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

Fortress provides \emph{comprehension} syntax, in which a generator clause list
binds values used in the body expression on the left-hand side of the
token \EXP{|}.  As described in \secref{generators}, each iteration of
the body expression must be assumed to execute in its own implicit
thread.  Comprehensions evaluate to aggregate values and have
corresponding aggregate types.  The rules for evaluation of a
comprehension are similar to those for a reduction expression (see
\secref{reduction-expr}).

The relationship between a comprehension and an aggregate expression (\secref{aggregate-expr}) is similar to the relationship between a reduction expression (\secref{reduction-expr}) and the corresponding infix operator application (\secref{operator-app-expr}).  The language does not enforce an explicit connection between comprehension syntax and the corresponding aggregate syntax, but in practice libraries that provide definitions for aggregate expressions are expected to define a corresponding comprehension and \emph{vice versa}.  As with reduction expressions, a comprehension using a particular set of enclosers corresponds to a call to a \emph{big bracketing operator}.  Thus the definition of set comprehensions is given by a function with the following signature:
%% opr BIG {[\T\] g:(Reduction[\R0\],T->R0)->R0}: Set[\T\]
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{BIG}} \{\llbracket{}T\rrbracket g\COLONOP(\TYP{Reduction}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket,T\rightarrow{}R_{0})\rightarrow{}R_{0}\}\COLON \TYP{Set}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)
\end{Fortress}
This is almost identical to the signature required to define a reduction
expression \EXP{\OPR{BIG}\:\emph{Op}}, shown in \secref{reduction-expr}.
Further information on defining comprehensions are described
in \secref{defining-generators}.

A set comprehension is enclosed in braces, with a left-hand body
separated by the token \EXP{|} from a generator clause list.
For example, the comprehension:
\input{\home/basic/examples/Expr.SetComp.tex}
evaluates to the set
\begin{Fortress}
\(\{0, 4, 16\}\)
\end{Fortress}

Map comprehensions are like set comprehensions,
except that the left-hand body must be of the form
\EXP{e_{1} \mapsto e_{2}}.
If \EXP{e_{1}} produces the same value but \EXP{e_{2}} a different value on more
than one iteration of the generator list,
a \TYP{KeyOverlap} exception is thrown.
For example:
\input{\home/basic/examples/Expr.MapComp.tex}
evaluates to the map
\begin{Fortress}
\(\{0 \mapsto 0, 4 \mapsto 8, 16 \mapsto 64\}\)
\end{Fortress}


List comprehensions are like set comprehensions,
except that they are syntactically enclosed in angle brackets.
For example:
\input{\home/basic/examples/Expr.ListComp.tex}
evaluates to the list
\begin{Fortress}
\(\langle 0, 4, 16 \rangle\)
\end{Fortress}
Note that the order of elements in the resulting list corresponds to
the \emph{natural order} of the generators in the generator clause
list (see \secref{defining-generators}).

component InferUnfixedFBoundedWalk
import Set.{...}
export Executable

(* A type parameter whose bound mentions itself and that nothing at a call fixes is left open under walk: every value is admitted where its type is expected, so a reduction with no static argument runs on its elements' own types. *)

trait Cmp[\T\] end

object BoxU[\T\]()
    getter kind(): String = "boxed"
end

mk[\T extends Cmp[\T\]\](): BoxU[\T\] = BoxU[\T\]()

run(): () = do
    r = SUM[j <- 0#4] (j / 2.0)
    assert(r, 3.0, "a sum of RR64 elements with no static argument joins its elements with their own + (reductions.tex, section \"Summations and Other Reduction Expressions\")")
    p = PROD[j <- 1#0] j
    assert(p, 1, "an empty product of ZZ32 elements with no static argument is the identity 1 (reductions.tex, section \"Summations and Other Reduction Expressions\")")
    lo = BIG MIN[j <- 0#4] (j - 2)
    assert(lo, -2, "BIG MIN with no static argument over j - 2 for j in 0#4 is -2 (reductions.tex, section \"Summations and Other Reduction Expressions\")")
    hi = BIG MAX[j <- 0#4] (j - 2)
    assert(hi, 1, "BIG MAX with no static argument over j - 2 for j in 0#4 is 1 (reductions.tex, section \"Summations and Other Reduction Expressions\")")
    s = { n^2 | n <- -2:2 }
    assert(|s|, 3, "a set comprehension with no static argument over n^2 for n in -2:2 holds three elements (comprehensions.tex, section \"Comprehensions\")")
    assert((0 IN s) AND (1 IN s) AND (4 IN s), true, "the set comprehension over n^2 for n in -2:2 holds 0, 1 and 4 (comprehensions.tex, section \"Comprehensions\")")
    b = mk()
    assert(b.kind, "boxed", "a call that fixes no static argument of a function whose type parameter's bound mentions itself runs, and its result answers its getter (inference.tex, section \"The Static Arguments of a Call\")")
    assert("ab.c".upto('.'), "ab", "String's upto answers the prefix before the character")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

(* An integer power answers its base's own type; at a negative exponent the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 throws DivisionByZero, and any other base throws IntegerOverflow, at an exponent of every integer type. *)
component IntegerPowerContractWalk
export Executable

overflows(f: () -> Any): Boolean =
  try
    ignore(f())
    false
  catch e
    IntegerOverflow => true
  end

dividesByZero(f: () -> Any): Boolean =
  try
    ignore(f())
    false
  catch e
    DivisionByZero => true
  end

shown(v: Any): String =
  typecase v of
    IntLiteral => v.asString || " : IntLiteral"
    ZZ32 => v.asString || " : ZZ32"
    ZZ64 => v.asString || " : ZZ64"

component OpenTupleDispatchWalk
export Executable

(* Under walk, a pair is not below a tuple type over a self-bounded type parameter that nothing fixed when overloads are compared, so the overload over Any runs, while a lone method over the tuple type runs for the pair. *)

object Holder[\T extends StandardTotalOrder[\T\]\]()
    pick(x: (T,T)): String = "tuple"
    pick(x: Any): String = "any"
    one(x: (T,T)): String = "one"
end

run(): () = do
    h = Holder()
    assert(h.pick((1, 2)), "any", "a pair given to pick, overloaded over a tuple of the unfixed parameter and over Any, runs the overload over Any")
    assert(h.one((1, 2)), "one", "a pair given to one, declared only over a tuple of the unfixed parameter, runs it")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

component OpenParameterListComprehensionWalk
import List.{...}
export Executable

(* Under walk, a list comprehension written at a self-bounded type parameter that nothing fixed ends in CastError, and so does a list's range subscript at stride 2 on a list of that open element type, while its subscript at stride 1 answers its elements. *)

trait SelfBound[\T\] end
object Leaf extends SelfBound[\Leaf\] end

emptyOf[\T extends SelfBound[\T\]\](): List[\T\] = <|[\T\] |>
copyOf[\T extends SelfBound[\T\]\](xs: List[\T\]): List[\T\] = <|[\T\] x | x <- xs |>

castErrorOf(f: () -> Any): Boolean =
  try
    ignore(f())
    false
  catch e
    CastError => true
  end

run(): () = do
    xs = emptyOf().addRight(Leaf).addRight(Leaf).addRight(Leaf)
    assert(|xs|, 3, "a list built from emptyOf, whose type parameter nothing fixes, holds the three elements added to it")
    assert(|xs[0#2]|, 2, "the list of the open element type at 0#2, stride 1, answers its first two elements")
    assert(castErrorOf(fn () => copyOf(xs)), true, "a list comprehension written at the open type parameter ends in CastError, where the open type admits every value checked against it (inference.tex, section \"The Static Arguments of a Call\")")
    assert(castErrorOf(fn () => xs[0:2:2]), true, "the list of the open element type at 0:2:2, stride 2, a comprehension written at the list's element type, ends in CastError")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The gap ledger's tool: it owns the ledger's format, reads its rows, and is
the only way to write them.

The ledger, explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md, is sorted into topic sections,
each a "## TITLE" heading over one table of rows. A row is one line of eight
cells, and keeps its number wherever it sits:

  | # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |

The template (POSITIONS.md, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is
explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md, 4.1):
  status       exactly one of POSITIVE-VERIFIED, NEGATIVE-VERIFIED,
               NEGATIVE-BOUNDED, CONTESTED, RETIRED, FIXED, DUPLICATE
  class        `kind (area)`, kind one of the legend's seven, area one of ten;
               `—` only for POSITIVE-VERIFIED and RETIRED
  spec         the .tex file and the section heading in quotes; a line number
               only against Specification-1.0-frozen/; `silent` where the
               specification does not say
  reproducer   one test (a name under the test folders, or a path) or probe
               path from the repository root, or `none`
  limits       row 1,200 characters, claim 300, reproducer 200, found by 60,
               notes 700
  a pipe inside a cell is written \\|

Cells are split only at a pipe that is not escaped as \\|. A row whose cells
hold bare pipes (the ledger had six) does not split into its table's width that
way; it is read by its split at pipes followed by a space or the line's end, as
facts-extract.py has always read it, and check reports it under `pipe`.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .ledger.lock beside the ledger), checks the
template on the line it writes, and puts the full earlier line of a row it
changes, unchanged, in the history file beside the ledger
(fortress-gap-ledger-history.md), under "### Row N" and a line saying what
became of it. A failed check prints the rules the row breaks and exits 1.
add, rewrite, close and duplicate check the whole line they write; note checks
only what it changes (the notes cell and the row's length), so that a row
failing the template elsewhere still takes a note. A row at its length limit
takes no note: rewrite cuts it back (the rework's decision D4, "each is cut
when next edited", process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md).

43:- P-46 **A conversion only makes a call possible: it never changes which declaration runs when one already fits.** The declaration that runs is chosen on the parameter types that each overload declares: first those that apply, then the most specific of them (P-45). A generic declaration applies if some type within its bounds takes the arguments. Only then is the chosen declaration instantiated by promotion: at the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce (P-74). So beside `op(a: Any, b: Any)`, `op[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T)` applies to a call with a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64`, at `T = Number`. It is the more specific, so it runs, at `ZZ64`. Why: the curator wants fast generic code that a JVM can specialise. His own broader rule is not taken: to apply any conversion that reaches a specific declaration, and to fall back to a plain one only when none does. Walk and the compiled checker both infer static arguments with coercion, by the same promotion. The compiled path inserts the conversions statically. P-49 gives the order in which the checker tries a call. Row 537: the compiled dispatch between two generic declarations of one name with different bounds.
45:- P-48 **A type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix takes its bound, never `Bottom`.** The arguments leave a parameter unfixed when it occurs only in the result type; when two arguments meet at it with no narrowest type into which both convert (a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` have one, `ZZ64`, by P-74); or when dispatch, at run time, picks a generic declaration and must choose the instance to run. Its instance is then the intersection of its upper bounds (`Any` if it has none). At checking, that is narrowed by what the call's expected type (P-49 defines it) requires of the declared return type; at run time, by the static type that the checker gave the call. It is never `Bottom`, never the union of the arguments' types, and never the value's type alone. The rule sets the instance, not which declaration runs (P-46). Why: the rule is the team's later word, from the POPL 2019 paper on multiple dispatch, and the curator trusts the team's later work above his own understanding (P-26). The rule changes nothing in microGPT, whose types are concrete. The library keeps the team's declarations of `fail`, `builtinPrimitive` and `List`'s empty comprehension, whose type parameters have no written bound, without the `extends Object` that a batch had added. Under walk, which has no static types, dispatch takes the value's type. Row 538: a compiled dispatcher that carries the static type that the checker gave the call, so that a generic declaration reached only at run time gets this instanc
46:- P-49 **The compiled checker tries a call first by subtyping, without the expected type, and coerces its arguments only when that attempt is not kept.** The expected type is the type that the call's context requires. The checker's first attempt checks the call by subtyping alone, without the expected type. It keeps that attempt when its result converts to the expected type, by coercion if need be. If it does not keep that attempt, it tries coercion of the arguments, with the expected type. So a declaration that fits the arguments as they are is not passed over for one that coercion reaches. Why: in the curator's words, coercion should be tried when there are no matches.
48:- P-51 **The checker retries a call written as another call's argument against each declaration's parameter type.** Take an outer call `f(g(x))`, whose argument is an inner call `g(x)`. If none of the compiled checker's attempts at the call accepts `f(g(x))` (P-49 gives the order of those attempts), the checker checks `g(x)` again, once for each declaration of `f`, with that declaration's parameter type at `g(x)`'s position as its expected type. Why: the curator wants the type inference rules unified across contexts, which covers cases that the team did not build. As built, a generic declaration of `f` is first instantiated from the other arguments. The declaration whose retry succeeds is kept, or the most specific of several; otherwise the call goes on as it would without the retry.
